Lecture 15 Sampling Distributions, the Sample Mean, the Central Limit Theorem and the Sample Proportion

What happens when you average copies of a random variable. The sample mean keeps the same centre , its spread shrinks to , and its histogram turns bell shaped as grows (the Central Limit Theorem). That lets the normal table answer questions about a sample mean, as in the salaries example. The last boards show that a sample proportion is a sample mean of zeros and ones.

Sampling Distributions

Given a random variable , we can use it to create a new random variable .

We will create copies [of] called and .

Definition

We then define as

Explanation (added) ✎

A copy of is a random variable with the same distribution as : the same possible values with the same probabilities, so the same mean and the same standard deviation. It is a separate measurement, though. and will usually come out as different numbers.

is built from random variables, so it is a random variable too. Its value is not known until the measurements are made. Capital is that random variable; the small from Lecture 2 is the number you get from one particular set of data. The distribution of is what the heading calls a sampling distribution.

is a linear combination, the same kind of object as in Lecture 14 with every coefficient equal to . That is why Lecture 14’s rules for and are all that sections 4 and 5 need.

In the photo, the wall clock, the speaker, the rolled-up projector screen and the head at the bottom are not content. The board reads “ copies ”; the word “of” is supplied.

Textbook Devore §5.3, p. 220, opening paragraph: before the data exist, each observation is a random variable, written . P. 221, Definition: a statistic is any quantity computed from sample data, and it is a random variable. P. 222: the distribution of a statistic is its sampling distribution. The board never uses the word “statistic”.

2Example: the weight of a whale

Example

Let measure the weight of a whale.

If we draw a simple random sample of size from our population of whales with replacement, we can create 3 copies of called and .

measure[s] the weight of the th whale selected.

gives the weight of the first whale.

gives the weight of the second whale.

gives the weight of the 3rd whale selected.

gives the mean weight of the three whales in the sample.

always gives the mean of the values assigned by and .

Explanation (added) ✎

Which whale is picked first is random, so the weight of the first whale is a random variable: that is . Because the whale goes back before the next pick (“with replacement”), the second pick is from the same full population, so has the same distribution as and does not depend on it. The same goes for .

Once the sample is taken you have three numbers and one number . Before it is taken you have three random variables and . Everything in this lecture is about before the sample is taken: where its values are centred, how spread out they are, and what shape their histogram has.

Textbook Devore §5.3, p. 220: the same point with the fuel efficiencies of two samples of three cars. Example 5.20 and Table 5.1 (pp. 220–221) list six samples of size 10 from one population and their six different sample means. The whales are not in the book.

3Samples from a population: independent, identically distributed

We often do this when we selected samples of size from a population. When we do this, gives the mean value that assigns to each sample member.

It gives the mean of the values assigned by and .

Definition

We call the random variable the sample mean.

Property

If we draw a simple random sample of size with replacement, the random variables and form a set of independent identically distributed random variables.

Explanation (added) ✎

“Independent identically distributed” is usually shortened to iid. It says two separate things, and each one is used once in the next two sections.

  • Identically distributed: every has the same distribution as . So and for every . This is what lets each be replaced by .
  • Independent: the result of one pick does not change the probabilities for any other pick. Sampling with replacement guarantees it (Lecture 6). This is what lets the variance of a sum be the sum of the variances (Lecture 14).

A simple random sample (Lecture 1) is one where every possible sample of that size is equally likely. Without replacement the picks are not exactly independent, but the 5% rule from Lectures 6 and 9 says the difference can be ignored when the sample is at most 5% of the population. The board comes back to this in section 9.

The board’s first sentence reads “the mean value that assigns to each sample member”. It means the mean of the values assigns to the sample members, which is what the board’s next sentence says.

Textbook Devore §5.3, p. 222, Definition: form a (simple) random sample if (1) they are independent and (2) every has the same distribution; “iid” is introduced in the next sentence. The same paragraph says the conditions hold exactly when sampling with replacement and approximately without replacement when .

Explanation (added) ✎

Line by line:

  1. Definition of .
  2. A constant comes out of a variance squared: with , so (Lecture 8).
  3. For independent random variables the variance of a sum is the sum of the variances (Lecture 14). On a test, this is the line that needs the word “independent” written beside it, as the board does.

What it says: averaging reduces spread. The variance is divided by , and the standard deviation by , not by . To cut in half you need four times as many observations. With the numbers of section 9, and give .

6Example: samples of size 2 from 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6

Example

Suppose we want to select samples of size 2 from the small population of 6 values listed: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6.

We will sample with replacement.

What does the distribution of sample means look like?

We can use the standard addition table we get when rolling two fair six sided dice to help construct the density histogram.

Explanation (added) ✎

Picking one value at random from 1 to 6 is one roll of a fair die, so the population has

Picking two values with replacement is two rolls: there are ordered samples, all equally likely (the multiplication rule from Lecture 4, and the two-dice grid from Lecture 6). The population is small enough that every sample can be listed, so the distribution of can be found exactly.

Textbook Not in the book. Devore §5.3, Example 5.21 (pp. 223–224) does the same thing with three prices that are not equally likely: Table 5.2 lists all nine samples of size 2, and Figure 5.8 (p. 224) draws the population and the histograms side by side.

Each of the 36 samples of size two we can select corresponds to a cell in the table.

Dividing the sum by 2 gives the sample mean.

Explanation (added) ✎

The column number is the first value picked, , and the row number is the second, . The cell holds , and . Cells with the same sum lie on a diagonal running from lower left to upper right, so counting a diagonal counts the samples with that mean: one cell for sum 2, two for sum 3, and so on up to six for sum 7, then back down to one for sum 12. Explanation (added) ✎

Why divide by the width. In a density histogram the area of a bar is the probability, not its height. The possible sample means are 0.5 apart, so each bar is 0.5 wide and its height has to be for the area to come back to . In Lecture 7 the bars were 1 wide, so height and probability were the same number. Using density is what lets histograms with different bar widths (section 7) be compared with one another and with a normal curve.

Explanation (added) ✎

Three things to see as goes 2, 4, 10:

  • The centre does not move. Every screen says Mean 3.500. That is from section 4.
  • The spread shrinks like . , , . That is from section 5. The bars also get taller, because the total area stays 1 while the histogram narrows.
  • The shape becomes a bell. One die is flat, two dice make a triangle, and by ten dice the bars are hard to tell from the normal curve. Nothing in sections 4 and 5 predicted this; it is the new fact, and section 8 states it as the Central Limit Theorem.

Why standardize. Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation gives every histogram mean 0 and standard deviation 1, whatever is. Centre and spread are then fixed, so the only thing left that can change with is the shape, and all the histograms can be compared with the one standard normal curve. The last screen is the starting point, . Use the widget below to watch the standardized histogram move toward the curve as grows.

8The Central Limit Theorem

The Central Limit Theorem

Theorem The Central Limit Theorem (CLT)

If and are independent identically distributed random variables, each with mean and standard deviation and

then

Explanation (added) ✎

What is inside the limit. is and is , from sections 4 and 5. So the fraction is standardized: the z-score move from Lecture 12, , applied to the sample mean with the sample mean’s own standard deviation.

What the “” means. is the standard normal random variable of Lecture 12. The statement is about distributions: as grows, the probabilities for the standardized sample mean get closer and closer to the probabilities for , so that approaches the table value for every . It is the last projector screen in motion: the standardized histogram settles onto the standard normal curve.

What it does not assume. Nothing is said about the shape of . The dice were flat; the salaries in section 9 are skewed. Only a mean, a standard deviation, and independent identically distributed copies are needed.

This board joins the theorem to sampling. A simple random sample gives independent identically distributed (section 3), which is exactly what the theorem asks for, so the theorem applies to the sample mean of a simple random sample. Compare the two z-scores:

The steps for a question about a sample mean:

  1. State why the normal approximation is allowed (the conditions; next board and section 9).
  2. Write the mean and the standard deviation of .
  3. Standardize with , not .
  4. Use the standard normal table, and write at the step where replaces the standardized .

Explanation (added) ✎

Normal . Lecture 14 ended with the fact that a linear combination of independent normal random variables is normal. is such a combination, with every coefficient , so it is exactly normal for , , or any . No approximation and no size condition. “Valid choice of ” means a whole number of at least 1.

The dice. One die is flat, which is not normal but is symmetric, and by the projector’s bars already follow the curve. That is the board’s second case.

Skewed . Skewness is what takes longest to average away, so this is where is used. Shapes from Lecture 2: unimodal means one peak; skewed to the right means a long tail to the right.

On a test, the condition is part of the answer: say which of these cases applies and why, before using the normal table.

The board’s “5 or 10” for unimodal, somewhat symmetric populations is not a number from the book.

9Example: the mean salary of 50 employees

Note

If we sample without replacement, just make sure the sample size is relatively small in comparison to the population size.

Example

At a large company, the average or mean yearly salary is $60 000 per year with a standard deviation of $20000 per year.

The distribution of yearly salarys is moderately skewed to the right.

Missing from the photos (added) ✎

No photo shows the line that states the question. From the working on the next two boards it was this, in my words: [a sample of 50 employees is selected; find the probability that the sample mean salary is more than $65 000, that is, ]. If your own notes have the exact wording, trust them.

Explanation (added) ✎

The note. Real samples of people are taken without replacement: nobody is picked twice. Then the are not exactly independent. If the sample is a small part of the population, removing a few people barely changes what is left, and the can be treated as independent. “Relatively small” is made exact on the next board with the 5% rule of Lectures 6 and 9.

The sketch. Skewed to the right pulls the mean to the right of the peak (Lecture 2), which is why the tick for 60000 is not under the highest point. Because of the skew, a question about one employee’s salary could not be answered with the normal table. A question about the mean of 50 can.

The board spells the plural “salarys”; it is typed as written.

Textbook Not in the book. The 5% condition is in Devore §5.3, p. 222: if , proceed as if the form a random sample.

Example continued: the conditions

Conditions:

Only moderately skewed: is probably large enough.

Sampling without replacement. Large company, probably more than 1000 employees. of the population size.

We can treat like a normal random variable with mean $60000 and standard deviation $2828.43.

Explanation (added) ✎

Two conditions, one for each thing the Central Limit Theorem needs.

  • Large enough for the shape. The population is skewed, so this is the case of section 8, and .
  • Independence. The sample is without replacement, so check the 5% rule: 5% of 1000 is 50, and the company is taken to have at least 1000 employees, so the sample of 50 is at most 5% of it.

Then the mean and standard deviation of from sections 4 and 5:

The words “probably” are the board’s: the question does not give the number of employees, so the board states the assumption it is making. Writing the conditions out like this is the justification the instructor marks.

Example continued: the probability
Explanation (added) ✎

Line 1 does the same thing to both sides of the inequality: subtract the mean of and divide by the standard deviation of . The right side is , rounded to 1.77 for the table.

Line 2 is where the Central Limit Theorem is used, and it is the reason for the : the standardized is treated like .

Line 3. The table gives areas to the left (Lecture 12), so a “greater than” probability is 1 minus the table value. Row 1.7, column .07 gives 0.9616.

Reading the answer. About 4 samples of 50 in every 100 would have a mean salary above $65 000. Compare one employee: $65 000 is only standard deviations above the mean, so salaries above $65 000 are common. A mean of 50 that high is unusual, because means vary much less than single values.

10The sample proportion

The Sample Proportion

Suppose we are looking at a population for which the proportion of the population with some property is .

If we sample with replacement and at each stage of the selection process, all population members are equal[ly] likely to be select[ed], then if counts the number of sample members selected with the property,

… [the photo was taken as this line was started; only the is written]

Explanation (added) ✎

The unfinished line is not in any other photo, so it is not completed here. What the setup gives, from Lecture 9: picks, each one a “success” (has the property) with the same probability , independent because the sampling is with replacement. That makes a binomial random variable, . The third board of this section uses exactly that when it writes as a sum of Bernoulli random variables.

is a fixed number that describes the population (a parameter, in the language of Lecture 2). , read “p hat”, will be the matching quantity for a sample.

To get the proportion of the sample with the property (the sample proportion), we divide the number of sample members with the property by the sample size .

Definition

If , the[n] gives the sample proportion.

The random variable is called the sample proportion.

Explanation (added) ✎

is to what is to : a random variable computed from the sample, whose value changes from sample to sample, used to estimate a fixed number that describes the population. If 50 people are sampled and 18 have the property, and .

The board reads “the gives”; “then” is meant.

Since

where the are independent Bernoulli random variables and each counts the number of success on the th trial,

we can view as a sample mean (it computes the mean from a sample of zeros and ones).

Explanation (added) ✎

A Bernoulli random variable (Lecture 9) takes the value 1 with probability and 0 with probability . There it was shown that and , and that a binomial is the sum of of them. So is the sample mean of independent identically distributed random variables that happen to take only the values 0 and 1.

12Lecture at a glance

Sample mean

A random variable. is one value of it.

Simple random sample, with replacement

are independent and identically distributed: each has mean and standard deviation .

Centre

Needs only “identically distributed”.

Spread

Needs independence.

Samples of size 2 from 1 to 6

36 samples, one per cell of the addition table. Sample mean = sum ÷ 2. Frequencies 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.

Density histogram

Area of a bar = relative frequency. Width 0.5 gives height .

Dice on the projector

Mean 3.500 every time. Standard deviation 1.208, 0.854, 0.540 for 2, 4, 10 dice. The shape becomes a bell.

Central Limit Theorem

For large enough , treat like a normal random variable with mean and standard deviation .

How large does n need to be

normal: any . unimodal and somewhat symmetric: or 10 is usually enough. Most distributions: . Without replacement: keep the sample at most 5% of the population.

Salaries
Sample proportion

The are independent Bernoulli random variables, so is a sample mean of zeros and ones.

  2. The four lengths turn out to be 32, 28, 35 and 29. Which symbol stands for the number 32, and what is ?

Show the worked answer

(a) gives the length of the third trout netted. Before the netting it is a random variable, because which trout comes up third is random.

(b) 32 is , the observed value of . The observed sample mean is

(c) is defined before any trout are netted, and its value depends on which four come up. Another four trout would give another value. is the one value this sample produced. The collection of all the values could take, with their probabilities, is its sampling distribution.

(d) Identically distributed: each has the same distribution as , so the same mean and standard deviation . True because every netting is from the same full population. Independent: the length of one trout does not change the probabilities for any other. True because each trout is put back first, so the sampling is with replacement.
